items.text: Deficiency means any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force or has been undertaken to be performed by a person in pursuance of a contract or otherwise in relation to any service.

items.text: Misleading advertisement in relation to any product or service means an advertisement, which falsely describes such product or service, or gives a false guarantee to, or is likely to mislead the consumers as to the nature, substance, quantity or quality of such product or service.

items.text: Unfair trade practice means a trade practice which, for the purpose of promoting the sale, use or supply of any goods or for the provision of any service, adopts any unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice including making false or misleading representation, refusal to refund paid consideration within 30 days, or disclosing confidential personal information.

items.text: Where the District Commission is satisfied that the goods complained against suffer from any of the defects specified in the complaint or that any of the allegations contained in the complaint about services or unfair trade practices are proved, it shall issue an order directing the opposite party to remove defects, replace goods with defect-free items, return the price paid along with interest, or pay compensation.

items.text: A product liability action may be brought by a complainant against a product manufacturer, product service provider, or product seller for any harm caused on account of a defective product. Facts: The consumer ordered a high-end laptop on an online e-commerce marketplace platform during a sale. Upon opening the sealed package, the consumer received a brick instead of the laptop. Issues: Whether an e-commerce marketplace platform can claim intermediary immunity when a wrong/defective product is delivered?; Whether non-refund by an online platform constitutes an Unfair Trade Practice under Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020?

Title: Triage this Indian IP/startup legal issue for a lawyer.
Court: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) / Court
Facts: Triage this Indian IP/startup legal issue for a lawyer.
Issues: ip_law
Provisions: Consumer Protection Act, 2019
Judgment: IP triage result: Do not treat this as one single IP claim yet. Split the matter into ownership, protectable subject matter, proof of copying/access, commercial harm, and remedy.

Fact pattern: a freelancer claims ownership over the website copy despite payment by the startup.

Potential routes: copyright for original expression, trademark or passing off for brand/source confusion, design/patent only if registration and subject matter support it, contract claim if an agreement controls ownership or confidentiality, and platform takedown as a fast non-litigation route.

Evidence pack: registration certificates or applications, source/design files, screenshots with URL and timestamp, domain and social handle records, invoices and publication history, assignment/licence agreements.

Questions to ask: Who created the asset? Was there an assignment? Was the asset published before? Is there registration? Is the allegedly copied material an idea, function, or original expression? Can access and similarity be shown?

Output for counsel: prepare a rights chart with asset, owner, proof, infringement theory, forum, interim relief possibility, and citation/source status. Do not cite cases unless verified.
